title: MOBA Games
description: Two teams of five, one map, and a race to destroy the enemy base: the MOBA is team strategy at its most layered. Players pick heroes with distinct roles, lane against opponents, farm gold and experience from map units, and spend that gold on items that reshape what their hero can do. Three lanes, a jungle, and defensive towers structure every match, and team fights decide the late game. No single player carries a match alone; composition, vision, and coordination win. Matches usually run twenty to forty minutes, and the genre's depth keeps it among the most watched in competitive gaming.

topics.History: The genre grew from player-made strategy maps into standalone games with professional leagues worldwide.
topics.Rules: Five against five, three lanes, towers, and a base to destroy. Gold and experience buy power through the match.
topics.Techniques: Farming, vision, team fights, and objective timing decide matches. Role discipline keeps a team coherent.
topics.Training: Lane drills, team-fight practice, draft preparation, and replay review build teams.

demo.code:
GOLD = [12000, 10500, 9800, 8700, 7200]
print("MOBA team gold example")
for i, g in enumerate(GOLD, 1):
    print("Player %d: %d gold" % (i, g))
print("Team total: %d gold" % sum(GOLD))
print("Average per player: %.0f gold" % (sum(GOLD) / len(GOLD)))

title: First-Person Shooters
description: See through the character's eyes, aim, move, and shoot: first-person shooters are the reflex genre of competitive gaming. Team formats, usually five against five, play short rounds in modes like bomb defusal and control points, and an in-game economy links rounds together: currency earned buys weapons and equipment next round. Crosshair placement, movement, and communication matter as much as raw aim, and professional teams add map strategy and utility planning. Reactions must be fast, but the best players win with positioning and information, not flick shots alone. Every round resets the test.

topics.History: The genre grew from 1990s action games into team competition with professional leagues.
topics.Rules: Short rounds, team modes, and a round-to-round economy structure matches. Currency buys weapons and equipment.
topics.Techniques: Aim, placement, movement, and communication decide rounds. Positioning beats raw reflexes over a series.
topics.Training: Aim drills, map work, economy planning, and communication practice build teams.

demo.code:
SHOTS = 100
HITS = 42
print("Aim accuracy example")
print("Shots: %d, hits: %d" % (SHOTS, HITS))
print("Accuracy: %.0f%%" % (HITS / SHOTS * 100.0))
print("Headshot example: 12 of 42 hits = %.0f%%" % (12 / 42 * 100.0))
demo.expected_output:
Aim accuracy example
Shots: 100, hits: 42
Accuracy: 42%
Headshot example: 12 of 42 hits = 29%

title: Real-Time Strategy
description: No turns, no pauses, and an opponent building an army at the same time: real-time strategy is multitasking under pressure. Players gather resources, expand bases, research technology, and fight for map control, all at once. The match flows from a quiet economy opening into clashes that can end in minutes or grind on. Top players issue hundreds of actions per minute, but speed alone does not win; scouting, build orders, and counters decide who has the right army at the right place. One against one, there is nowhere to hide: every mistake is visible, and every decision is yours.

topics.History: The genre grew from 1990s strategy games into one-against-one competition with international tournaments.
topics.Rules: Build, gather, research, and fight in real time. Victory comes from destroying the opponent or meeting the set condition.
topics.Techniques: Economy, scouting, build orders, and army control decide matches. Actions per minute measure speed, not judgement.
topics.Training: Build-order drills, multitasking practice, and replay study build competitive players.

demo.expected_output:
Strategy economy example
Minerals: 1200
Gas: 600

title: Fighting Games
description: One against one, best of rounds, and a contest of reading minds: fighting games are the purest competitive duel in gaming. Players control fighters with distinct moves, and matches turn on spacing, timing, and punishment: attack at the wrong moment and the opponent answers with a combo. Frame data, the exact timing of every move, lets top players find advantages measured in hundredths of a second. Tournaments are famous for open brackets, where an unknown entrant can meet a world champion in the first round. The genre rewards study, nerve, and adaptation across a series.

topics.History: The genre grew from arcade play into global tournaments known for open brackets.
topics.Rules: Rounds decide matches; health bars and timeouts govern round wins. Series are best-of sets.
topics.Techniques: Spacing, timing, and reading the opponent matter most. Combos punish mistakes; matchup knowledge guides picks.
topics.Training: Combo drills, frame-data study, matchup practice, and long sets build competitors.

demo.code:
HEALTH = 100
DAMAGE = [12, 18, 22, 15]
print("Fighting game combo example")
print("Starting health: %d" % HEALTH)
for i, d in enumerate(DAMAGE, 1):
    HEALTH -= d
    print("Hit %d: %d damage, health left: %d" % (i, d, HEALTH))
print("Total combo damage: %d" % sum(DAMAGE))
demo.expected_output:
Fighting game combo example
Starting health: 100
Hit 1: 12 damage, health left: 88
Hit 2: 18 damage, health left: 70
Hit 3: 22 damage, health left: 48
Hit 4: 15 damage, health left: 33
Total combo damage: 67

title: Sports Simulations
description: Real sports, played on screen: sports simulations recreate football, basketball, racing, golf, and more, with seasons, tournaments, and team management built in. Players control athletes or whole squads, and competitive modes run from one-against-one matches to leagues and management contests. The genre draws fans of the real sport who want to play it all year, and its calendar often follows the real season. Skill blends game knowledge with real-sport understanding: tactics, timing, and execution under pressure. The best players study both the game and the sport it mirrors.

topics.History: The genre grew from early sports titles into annual franchises with leagues that follow real sporting calendars.
topics.Rules: Game rules mirror the modelled sport, with seasons and tournaments organising competition.
topics.Techniques: Tactics, timing, and execution decide matches. Knowledge of the real sport transfers directly.
topics.Training: Mechanics drills, tactical study, and ranked play build competitors.

demo.code:
SEASON_GAMES = 38
WINS = 24
DRAWS = 8
LOSSES = 6
print("Sports simulation season example")
print("Games: %d, wins: %d, draws: %d, losses: %d" % (SEASON_GAMES, WINS, DRAWS, LOSSES))
print("Points (3 per win, 1 per draw): %d" % (WINS * 3 + DRAWS))
print("Win rate: %.1f%%" % (WINS / SEASON_GAMES * 100.0))
demo.expected_output:

title: Battle Royale
description: A hundred players, one shrinking zone, one survivor: battle royale games start everyone equal and let the map decide the rest. Players land, loot weapons and equipment, and move as the safe zone shrinks, forcing fights. Decisions matter as much as aim: where to land, what to carry, when to fight, when to rotate. Squads of two to four add revival and coordination, sharing loot and covering angles. No two matches play the same, because loot, zone, and encounters all vary. The winner is usually the player or team that positions best in the final circles.

topics.History: The genre grew from survival mods in the 2010s into a dominant competitive format.
topics.Rules: Many players, one map, a shrinking zone, and a last-team-standing win condition define the format.
topics.Techniques: Looting, positioning, rotation timing, and aim decide matches. The final circles reward patience and angles.
topics.Training: Landing drills, rotation practice, and endgame review build competitors.

title: Card Battlers
description: Build a deck, manage resources, and outplay an opponent card by card: card battlers are strategy in miniature. Cards represent creatures, spells, and effects, played with mana that grows each turn, so every turn is a spending decision. Deck building matters before the match starts; reading the opponent matters during it. New card releases regularly reshape the best decks, so the game never stands still. Ranked ladders and tournaments structure competition. The genre rewards planning and probability sense, because every hand differs and adaptation beats any fixed plan.

topics.History: The genre descends from physical trading card games, adapted to digital play with ladders and tournaments.
topics.Rules: Decks, growing mana, and health totals structure duels. New releases reshape the card pool regularly.
topics.Techniques: Deck choice, mana spending, and reading the opponent decide matches. Probability sense guides risky lines.
topics.Training: Deck testing, card-pool study, and match review build competitors.

title: Racing Simulations
description: Real tracks, real physics, and races run like real motorsport: racing simulations are the bridge between gaming and the circuit. Players use wheels, pedals, and rigs, learning braking points, lines, and setup exactly as real drivers do. Online races, leagues, and championships mirror real formats with qualifying and pit stops, and some real drivers train in simulation. The skill is consistency: fast over a full race, clean in traffic, and smart on strategy. One quick lap proves little; a clean, fast race distance proves everything. The genre's top events demand professional preparation.

topics.History: The genre grew from arcade driving games into realistic simulations with leagues and professional competition.
topics.Rules: Qualifying, grid starts, pit stops, and driving standards mirror real motorsport.
topics.Techniques: Lines, braking, setup, and racecraft decide races. Consistency over distance beats one fast lap.
topics.Training: Track practice, telemetry study, and league racing build sim drivers.

title: Rhythm Games
description: Notes arrive on a track, and the player hits them in time: rhythm games turn music into a competitive test of timing and stamina. Score attack on set songs is the standard format, with charts from gentle beginner patterns to expert tracks demanding hundreds of inputs per minute. Timing windows grade each hit from perfect to miss, and combos multiply scores until a miss breaks them. Communities extend every game with custom songs and charts, so the catalogue never ends. The core test is instantly clear to a newcomer, which makes the genre one of the most accessible in competitive gaming.

topics.History: The genre grew from arcade music machines into console, handheld, and mobile competition.
topics.Rules: Notes, timing windows, combos, and grades structure scoring. Misses break combos.
topics.Techniques: Timing, reading speed, coordination, and stamina decide scores. Harder charts demand all four.
topics.Training: Gradual speed increases, pattern drills, and stamina work build rhythm players.

print("Notes per beat: %.1f" % (NOTES_PER_MIN / BPM))

title: Speedrunning
description: Finish the game as fast as humanly possible: speedrunning turns any game into a race against the clock and the leaderboard. Categories split the contest, main story, all items, or special conditions, and times are verified by video under community rules. Runners dissect games frame by frame, hunting shortcuts and optimal routes, then practise segments thousands of times. One mistake can kill a record run, which is why the discipline demands patience as much as skill. Live events gather runners for charity, and leaderboards record the fastest verified times per game and category.

topics.History: The practice grew from demo scenes and video sharing into a global community with live charity events.
topics.Rules: Categories and video verification govern records. Each game community sets its own rules.
topics.Techniques: Route knowledge, precise execution, and nerve under record pressure decide runs.
topics.Training: Segment practice and repeated full attempts build speedrunners.

print("Improvement from first attempt: %d seconds" % (RUNS[0] - BEST))

title: Mobile Esports
description: Competitive gaming on the device in your pocket: mobile esports adapts MOBA, shooter, battle royale, and card genres to touch controls and shorter matches. Growth has been fastest where the phone is the main gaming device, with major tournaments, regional leagues, and professional teams built around mobile titles. Virtual joysticks, touch aiming, and custom layouts replace keyboard and mouse, and matches run shorter to fit mobile sessions. The scale is vast, because phones outnumber every other gaming device, and many mobile competitors have never owned a PC or console.

topics.History: The platform grew with smartphones into tournaments and leagues where phones dominate gaming.
topics.Rules: Genre rules apply per title, adapted for touch and shorter sessions.
topics.Techniques: Touch control, layout optimisation, and fast decisions decide mobile matches.
topics.Training: Control drills, ranked play, and team review build mobile competitors.

title: VR Esports
description: Headset on, controllers in hand, and your body is the controller: VR esports turns physical movement into competitive play. Shooters, sports, rhythm, and strategy titles adapt to room-scale spaces, and competitions run in tracked arenas or at home. Fitness matters here in a way other genres do not demand: players duck, dodge, and aim with their whole bodies, so matches run shorter to manage fatigue. The scene is younger and smaller than PC or mobile competition, but it is growing, and it hints at a future where competitive gaming is genuinely physical.

topics.History: The platform grew with consumer headsets in the late 2010s into arena and online events.
topics.Rules: Title rules apply, played in tracked spaces with headset and controller tracking.
topics.Techniques: Movement, spatial awareness, and motion aiming decide VR matches. Stamina limits match length.
topics.Training: Movement drills, tracked-space practice, and fitness work build VR competitors.

title: Coaching and Analytics
description: Behind every top team is a staff: coaches who set strategy, analysts who read the data, and performance staff who manage training and health. Analysts turn match data into patterns, which maps favour which strategies, where rounds are lost, how opponents behave under pressure, and coaches turn patterns into practice. Replay review, targeted drills, and opponent-specific plans mirror traditional sport. The field has professionalised fast, and the gap between good teams and great ones is often coaching, not talent. A team that learns faster than its rivals improves faster than its rivals.

topics.History: Coaching grew from captains into professional staffs as competition matured, adding analysts and performance roles.
topics.Rules: Match communication rules for coaches vary by title and event and must be followed.
topics.Techniques: Data analysis, replay review, draft prep, and practice design are the staff's core skills.
topics.Training: Match study, opponent profiles, and targeted drills turn analysis into improvement.

demo.expected_output:

title: Tournament Formats
description: Single elimination, double elimination, round robin, Swiss: formats are the architecture of competition, and each tells a different story. One loss ends a single-elimination run; double elimination grants a second chance through a lower bracket; round robin has every team meet every other; Swiss pairs teams with similar records each round. Leagues stretch over weeks, cups compress into days. Format shapes outcomes: single elimination crowns peak performance, double elimination rewards consistency, round robin rewards depth, and Swiss balances fairness with length. Choosing a format is choosing what kind of champion an event produces.

topics.History: Formats were borrowed from traditional sport and chess and adapted to online play and big fields.
topics.Rules: Progression, elimination, and seeding rules are published before play. Tiebreakers resolve standings.
topics.Techniques: Seeding, bracket design, scheduling, and tiebreakers are the organiser's skills.
topics.Training: Bracket simulation and schedule planning prepare organisers for real events.

print("Round robin example")

print("Matches (each pair once): %d" % (TEAMS * (TEAMS - 1) // 2))
print("Matches per team: %d" % (TEAMS - 1))
demo.expected_output:

title: Broadcast and Production
description: What the audience sees is a production, not just a game: observers steer the camera, commentators explain the action, analysts break down strategy, and directors cut between game, studio, and crowd. Overlays carry scores, statistics, and player cameras, and replays catch the moments live viewers missed. Major events fill arenas and stream to huge online audiences, and production quality now matches traditional sports television. The craft is timing: showing the right fight, the right reaction, and the right replay at the right moment. Good production makes a complex game readable to a newcomer.

topics.History: Broadcasting grew from community streams into professional arena productions with dedicated observer teams.
topics.Rules: Stream delay rules prevent teams gaining information from the broadcast.
topics.Techniques: Observation, commentary, analysis, directing, and graphics are the production crafts.
topics.Training: Show rehearsals, camera practice, and broadcast review build production teams.

title: Fair Play and Anti-Cheat
description: Competition is only meaningful if it is honest, and esports protects that with anti-cheat software, integrity rules, and conduct standards. Anti-cheat tools watch for unauthorised programs such as aimbots and wallhacks, while tournaments add referees, controlled player areas, and equipment checks. Cheating brings bans, forfeited prizes, and disqualification, and the gravest integrity cases reach organisers and, where the law applies, legal authorities. Fair play goes beyond software: it is sportsmanship, respect for opponents and officials, and honest play when nobody is watching. The systems exist so that results mean something.

topics.History: Anti-cheat grew with online gaming into dedicated software and integrity programmes.
topics.Rules: Unauthorised assistance, match-fixing, and leaks are banned, with bans, forfeits, and disqualification as penalties.
topics.Techniques: Software detection, refereeing, equipment checks, and education protect competition.
topics.Training: Rule briefings and integrity training prepare players and staff before events.

print("Flagged cases go to human review, not automatic penalty")
demo.expected_output:
